latest.content:
26 Aug 2026 09:00
RNS Number : 1345S
Hammerson PLC
26 August 2026
Hammerson plc (the 'Company')
Dividend Currency Conversion Announcement
26 August 2026
On 30 July 2026, the Company announced that the Board of Directors had declared an interim dividend of 9.67 pence per ordinary share ('Share') for the period ending 31 December 2026 (the 'Interim 2026 Dividend')
.
The Interim 2026 Dividend will be treated as a Property Income Distribution ('PID') and will be subject to a 20% UK withholding tax unless exemptions apply.
The Company will not be offering a scrip dividend alternative but, for shareholders who wish to receive their dividend in the form of Shares, the Dividend Reinvestment Plan ('DRIP') will be available. The terms and conditions of the DRIP can be found at
https://uk.investorcentre.mpms.mufg.com/Login/Login
.
Shareholders registered on the South African Branch Register should contact their CSDP or Broker for further information.
The Interim 2026 Dividend is payable on Thursday, 15 October 2026 to shareholders registered on the UK principal register ('UK Shareholders') and the South African branch register ('SA Shareholders') who have elected to receive the dividend in cash. The Record Date for both UK Shareholders and SA Shareholders is at the close of business on Friday, 4 September 2026. The DRIP purchases settlement date (subject to market conditions and the purchase of shares in the open market) is Monday, 19 October 2026 in the UK and Thursday, 29 October 2026 in South Africa.
The Interim 2026 Dividend should be regarded as a "foreign dividend" for SA income and SA dividend tax purposes
and the funds will be paid from the United Kingdom
.
Shareholders receiving the Interim 2026 Dividend in cash
The Company confirms that the South African Rand rate for the Interim 2026 Dividend will be ZAR 21.7444 to GBP 1, which is the rate determined on Tuesday, 25 August 2026. The Interim 2026 Dividend is payable in South African Rand to SA Shareholders. Shareholders who do not elect the DRIP will be paid as follows:

Cash PIDs
The information below is intended as a general guide only and is based on Hammerson's understanding of the law and practice currently in force. The Company accepts no responsibility for such general guidance and any shareholder who is in any doubt as to their tax position should seek independent professional advice.
The Interim 2026 Dividend should be regarded as a "foreign dividend" for SA income tax and dividends tax purposes.
A 20% UK withholding tax is applicable to the Interim 2026 dividend as it will be paid as a PID. After payment of the PID, qualifying South African shareholders may apply to HMRC for a refund of the difference between the 20% UK withholding tax deducted and the UK/South African Double Tax Treaty rate of 15%, i.e. 5% of the tax withheld.
The Interim 2026 cash dividend will be exempt from SA income tax but it will be subject to SA Dividends Tax as it will be declared in respect of a share listed on the exchange operated by the JSE. SA Dividends Tax will apply to the Interim 2026 cash dividend, at a rate of 20%, unless the beneficial owner of the dividend is exempt from SA Dividends Tax or qualifies for a reduction of the SA Dividends Tax liability to 5% (if they can claim a credit for the effective 15% UK withholding tax suffered against the 20% SA Dividends Tax rate). The applicability of the exemption or reduced rate will be subject to the prescribed requirements for effecting the exemption or reduction being in place by the requisite date.
Shareholders electing the DRIP
Partial elections are not permitted under the DRIP.
SA Shareholders electing the DRIP should note that, in respect of fractional entitlements that may arise, all allocations of shares will be rounded down to the nearest whole number, and any residual amounts that are not used to reinvest in shares (as a result of rounding down) will be paid out to these SA Shareholders in cash.
It is the Company's understanding that the residual cash paid to SA Shareholders who have made DRIP elections would already have been taxed prior to the calculation of the number of shares and any residual cash owing to such SA Shareholders. Accordingly, no further tax should be payable on the cash paid to SA Shareholders as a result of any fractional entitlements.
The above information and the guidelines on the taxation of dividends are provided as a general guide based on the Company's understanding of the law and practice currently in place. Any shareholder who is in any doubt as to their tax position should seek independent professional advice.

company_30s.what_they_do: Hammerson plc owns and manages a portfolio of high‑profile shopping centres across the UK.  The business earns from leasing retail space, operating ancillary services and occasionally selling or redeveloping sites.
company_30s.why_they_matter: The company sits at the heart of the UK retail landscape, providing anchor tenants for major brands and generating steady rental income.  Its properties are in prime locations that attract both shoppers and investors, giving it a defensible niche in an industry still adjusting to post‑pandemic consumer habits.
company_30s.current_state: Hammerson is in a transition phase: it has sold non‑core assets, taken on new equity to fund an acquisition, issued a bond, and is repurchasing shares.  The stock is trading at a steep discount to its historic highs, signalling a deep market sell‑off.

rns_narrative: Hammerson has been actively reshaping its balance sheet – selling £69 m of non‑core property to finance a 50 % stake in Ilac, issuing a EUR350 m bond, and launching a retail‑only placement to raise fresh equity.
The company is also returning cash to shareholders with a dividend and a share‑repurchase programme, which signals confidence in its cash‑flow generation.
Together these moves suggest a strategy of consolidating core assets, injecting capital for growth, and rewarding investors while tightening its capital structure.

crowd_tape.dominant_theme: Quiet optimism – traders are watching but not yet vocal, leaving room for a surprise bounce.
crowd_tape.bull_narrative: A handful of posts praise the new Ilac stake and the placement as evidence of a rebound, hinting that insiders expect the equity to lift the stock.
crowd_tape.bear_narrative: Some chatter flags the long lock‑up on the retail offer and worries that the bond could dilute equity, but overall bearish voices are sparse.
crowd_tape.sentiment_shift: The tone has shifted from neutral to mildly bullish in the last week, driven by the announcement of the Ilac purchase and the placement.

whats_happening_now.attention_check: Google Trends is flat – no public interest spikes, so a news event could trigger a big surprise move.

near_term_catalysts: Completion of the retail‑only placement – if the company raises the expected £120 m, it will reduce debt and fund the Ilac acquisition.
First dividend payment – a timely payout can lift sentiment and attract income‑seeking investors.
Bond maturity or refinancing – if the company successfully rolls over the EUR350 m debt at a lower rate, it will improve cash‑flow and lower risk.
Share‑repurchase acceleration – a sudden spike in buying back shares can support the price and signal confidence.
expect_next.watch_for: Look for a volume spike above the 20‑day average on the day of the placement announcement, a price break above the recent low, and a clear statement from management confirming the Ilac stake is in place.
expect_next.timing_regime: The stock sits in the early recovery stage of a deep crash.  APEX compression suggests a tight range; the next move will likely be a breakout if the placement is successful and the dividend is paid.

buy_vs_sell.bull_case: The company is at a very low point in its cycle, and the recent equity placement plus the Ilac acquisition provide a clear catalyst for a rebound.  Historically, deep‑crash bottoms have returned 30‑50% once the catalyst is triggered.  If the stock recovers to the midpoint of its 52‑week range, that would be a 200‑plus% gain over the current level.
buy_vs_sell.bear_case: If the placement fails to raise the target or the bond is not refinanced, the company could face liquidity pressure.  A failure to deliver dividends or a halt in the share‑repurchase would cap upside and keep the price stuck at the current low.
buy_vs_sell.risk_reward: Potential upside is >200% if the price moves to the 52‑week midpoint.  The maximum loss is the entire position if the company remains stuck in the deep‑crash zone.  The asymmetry is roughly 1:3 – you could lose 100% to gain 200%.

playbook.if_bullish: Enter when the price breaks the 20‑day high with volume >1.5× average.  Size 2–3 % of the portfolio and set a stop 15–20 % below the entry to protect against a false breakout.
playbook.if_watching: Hold a small position (1–2 %) until the placement announcement is made and the price confirms a breakout.  If volume spikes and the price moves above the recent high, add the full size.
playbook.if_passing: No terminal risks identified; the company has not been delisted or declared bankruptcy.  The only downside is the risk that the placement does not close, which would keep the stock in a deep‑crash state.

ai_insights.bottom_line: Hammerson sits at a deep crash level, poised for a rebound once the new equity placement and Ilac acquisition materialise – a high‑reward, asymmetric play that rewards patience.
